usage_notes.narrative: Benson assigns maj7 (and its enharmonic companions Em7 and Am7) to the Root/Tonic region -- the region of rest -- in major keys. "Root Region Chords (Tonic): Cmaj7 (I), Em7 (IIIm), Am7 (VIm)." Any maj7 chord may therefore be freely substituted by any other Root-region chord. Chapter 1, p. 1.

Benson catalogues the full palette of available voicing tensions over a major 7th chord: Cmaj7, Cmaj7(9), C6, C6(9), Cmaj7(#11), C6(#11), C6(9)#11, Cmaj7(6), Cmaj7(6)9. The player should select among these colours according to what the melody permits during comping. Chapter 1, p. 2.

Over a Cmaj7 chord (or any chord belonging to the major scale), Benson prescribes using G major pentatonic quartal voicings, C major pentatonic quartal voicings, or a mixture of both. The F major pentatonic is excluded because it contains the avoid note F. Chapter 6, p. 210.

For a lydian colour over Cmaj7, Benson prescribes borrowing quartal chords from B minor pentatonic or D major pentatonic via modal interchange. "To create a lydian sound over Cmaj7 chord for example, we use quartal chords belonging to 'B' minor pentatonic scale, or 'D' major pentatonic scale." Chapter 6, p. 263.

When comping over a maj7 chord, Benson rules that "the most important thing when comping is to follow the melody, which will 'tell' us what the best chord options are." When improvising, however, the player may freely choose among all learned colour extensions. Chapter 1, p. 4.

Benson places min7 chords across multiple harmonic regions. In major keys, Em7 (IIIm) and Am7 (VIm) are Root/Tonic-region members; Dm7 (IIm) is a major Subdominant-region member. In minor keys, Cm7 (I) is the tonic. Same-region interchangeability governs all substitutions. Chapter 1, pp. 1 and 4.

Benson lists the full tension palette for minor 7th chords: Cm7, Cm7(9), Cm7(11), Cm7(9)11, Cm(maj7)9, Cm6, Cm6(9). The melody always determines which of these is usable when comping; all are available when improvising. Chapter 1, p. 2.

Benson teaches that the IIm7 chord replaces IVmaj7 as the standard subdominant partner in the II/V/I cadence because both belong to the same Subdominant region. "Notice that we had to replace the IVth degree by the IIm, which belongs to the same region." This is the foundational rationale for the II/V/I itself. Chapter 1, p. 3.

Benson prescribes dorian quartal voicings primarily for static-harmony contexts. "Usually the dorian chords are related to static harmonies. However, they can be a tremendous asset when used over non traditional harmonic situations, giving a dorian modal vibe to the chord." Chapter 7, p. 279.

When a tritone substitution is applied over the IIm7 in a major II/V/I (e.g., Gm7 | C7(9) | Fmaj7 -> Gm7(11) | Gb7(#11) | Fmaj7), Benson requires adjusting the IIm7 voicing as well. "We should also change the voicing from the 1st chord as well. Therefore, we would have: || Gm7(11) | Gb7(#11) | Fmaj7 ||." Chapter 1, p. 14.

Benson includes Cm(maj7)9 in the tension palette for minor 7th chords (listed under minor 7th voicing possibilities). In minor II/V/I contexts, the tonic minor chord may be voiced as min(maj7) with the 9th added. Chapter 1, p. 2.

In the F melodic minor quartal family over Dø, Benson notes that the first degree chord Fm(maj7)add4 "sometimes can be replaced by a chord not belonging to that family: D#/E, which is actually a F#7(13)b9 over E. This is not a rule, it is just a chord voicing that works well with the other voicings even though it does not belong to this chord family." Chapter 7, p. 277.

Benson places the half-diminished chord (Bø / Dø) in the Dominant region as the VII degree: "Dominant Region Chords: G7 (V), Bø (VII)." In minor keys, Dø also serves as the II degree in the Subdominant region. Chapter 1, pp. 1 and 4.

Benson lists the tension palette for half-diminished chords: Dø, Dø(9), Dø(11), Dø(9)11, Dm7(b6). The Dm7(b6) variant is the enharmonic of the half-diminished and underscores the locrian-major-2nd reading. Chapter 1, p. 2.

In a minor II/V/I (e.g., Dø/G7/Cm7), Benson prescribes treating Dø as the VI degree of F melodic minor (locrian major 2nd). This dual membership unlocks F melodic minor's entire chord family as a substitution resource over the IIø without altering cadential function. "If we consider Dø chord as being locrian major 2nd we will have the VIth degree of F melodic minor." Chapter 3, p. 47.

Benson specifies three quartal chord families usable over a half-diminished chord: one derived from Eb major (gives locrian sound), one from Db major (re-frames the chord as D7(#9) via tritone substitution logic, giving blues vibe), and one from F melodic minor (because Dø is the VI degree of that scale). Chapter 7, p. 275.

Benson prescribes a specific transformation for the Db major quartal family over Dø: "we transformed the Dø into D7(#9) chord, giving it a blues vibe. Then using the tritone substitution for D7(#9), we can find Ab7(13), that we can consider mixolydian. Therefore, having this mixolydian chord, we can find the 'Db' major scale quartal chord voicings." Chapter 7, p. 275.

Benson demonstrates analytically that the major II (Dm7 / dorian) and the minor II (Bø) are "the same" because the third inversion of Dm6 is Bø: "the third inversion of Dm6 is Bø which is the II degree from the Am cadence. So we conclude that both II degree are the same." Chapter 1, p. 6.

Benson assigns dom7 (G7, V degree) to the Dominant region, whose function is "the sense of tension and instability, and wants to resolve to the tonic." Dominant and subdominant region chords are also declared interchangeable for purposes of delay and color. Chapter 1, pp. 1 and 8.

For the V7 chord leading to a major tonic, Benson catalogues the full tension palette: G7, G7(9), G7(b9), G7(#9), G7(13), G7(b13), G7(b9)b13, G7(#9)b13, G7(9)13, G7(b9)13, G7(#11), G7(b9)#11, Gsus9, Gsus13, Gsus(b9). Melody determines which tension is appropriate when comping. Chapter 1, p. 2.

Benson defines tritone substitution as replacing any dom7 with the dom7 a tritone away from its root: "if the chord is G7, the replacement will be Db7. The reason we can do this exchange is that both have the same tritone." The substituted chord shares the original tritone and is therefore functionally equivalent. Chapter 1, p. 13.

When a tritone substitution sounds poor with its original tension, Benson prescribes adjusting both the tritone chord's extension and the preceding IIm7 voicing together. Example: C7(9) -> Gb7(b13) fails; use Gb7(#11) instead, and change the preceding Gm7 to Gm7(11): "|| Gm7(11) | Gb7(#11) | Fmaj7 ||." Chapter 1, p. 14.

Benson prescribes secondary dominants as dom7 chords that resolve to non-tonic scale degrees, assigned solely by their resolution target: "secondary dominants are dominant chords that resolve to the other harmonic field degrees. They don't belong to the harmonic field and have nothing to do with it, except for the chord that they were assigned to resolve to." Chapter 1, p. 7.

Benson prescribes substituting VII7 for V7 on the basis of chromatic voice-leading: "all the notes of B7 can work as leading tones to the notes of C6, because they are half step from each other, creating a sensation of tension and resolution." The V/I motion (G7, C6) may be replaced by VII7/I (B7, C6). Chapter 2, p. 20.

In blues and Brazilian music contexts, Benson prescribes converting every chord in a turnaround to dominant 7th: "all the chords of the turnaround become dominant with different voicings. Each dominant chord is leading to the next chord until it finally leads to the tonic key (I)." Chapter 4, p. 83.

Benson notes that in a minor II/V/I (e.g., Aø | D7(b9) | Gm7), applying a tritone substitution over the dominant yields Ab7(#11), and "the voicings work perfect and we do not have to change anything." This contrasts with major II/V/I where tensions in the tritone sub are optional. Chapter 2, p. 17.

Benson corrects his own pedagogical simplification (altering only dominant chords leading to minor degrees) and states the real rule: "we can use any alteration to any dominant chord leading to major or minor. However, we must make sure the altered notes we choose can be applied over the song we are playing, because the melody will always determine what we can and can not use." Chapter 1, p. 10.

Benson prescribes that a Fake Diminished chord -- an inverted dom7(b9) with the root removed -- can substitute directly for the V7 chord. For example, an A7(b9) yields four diminished inversions (C#°, E°, G°, Bb°) each usable as a dominant substitute. "This type of diminished chord can be analyzed as an inverted dominant 7th (b9) chord." Chapter 2, p. 19.

Benson prescribes that the V7 chord in a minor cadence almost always takes altered tensions: "the dominant seventh chords almost always use altered tensions such as: b9, #9, #11, b13. The major 13th can be used with some regularity in the chords, but it is still an exception. In the key of Cm we can have the cadence: G7(b9)13 leading to Cm7 for example." Chapter 1, p. 4.

Benson identifies dom7(b9) chords (7, b9, 3 intervals from low to high without the root) as the structural basis of Fake Diminished chords. "Notice that dominant 7th chords such as 7(b9), 7(#9), and 7(b13), can be considered as being the same, therefore they have the same function." Chapter 1, p. 14.

In a minor II/V/I (Dø/G7/Cm7), Benson prescribes treating G7 as an altered chord -- "the VIIth degree of Ab melodic minor" -- which unlocks the entire Ab melodic minor chord family as a substitution resource over the dominant. Chapter 3, p. 47.

Benson prescribes treating a dom7alt chord as locrian (its arpeggio is half-diminished) to unlock the major scale a half-step above as a quartal voicing source: "the scale arpeggio of a dominant 7th altered chord is half diminished, we can consider it for a while as being locrian, which allows us to use all the chords built from the major scale that generates it. In the case of 'G' locrian, we could use all the chords built from the 'Ab' major scale over it." Chapter 6, p. 254.

Over dom7alt (Locrian) quartal voicings, Benson warns that the minor pentatonic fails because "the perfect 5th of the scale does not belong to this mode." The fix: use the minor blues scale instead, emphasizing the #4. Chapter 6, p. 226.

Unlike the minor pentatonic (which fails over Locrian quartal voicings due to the perfect 5th), the minor blues scale with emphasis on #4 may be used over dom7alt Locrian voicings without modal conflict. "In order to solve this problem, we can play the Minor Blues scale over Locrian chord voicings emphasizing the #4." Chapter 6, p. 226.

Any dom7 that is neither the V degree nor a tritone substitution is classified as lydian dominant and must be tensioned with 9, 13, or #11: "Dominant 7th chords that are not the Vth degree or a tritone substitution, are always considered lydian dominant. In other words, we can use the following tensions on them: 9, 13, or #11." Chapter 1, p. 2.

Benson places a strict restriction on lydian dominant (mixolydian #4) quartal voicings: "It can only be used over dominant 7th chords that are not leading to any other chord. The only exception is when we have a sequence of many dominant 7th chords one after another." Chapter 7, p. 279.

Unlike the general ban on lydian dominant quartal voicings over resolving dominants, when every chord in a progression is dominant one after another, lydian dominant quartal voicings may be used throughout the chain. "The only exception is when we have a sequence of many dominant 7th chords one after another." Chapter 7, p. 279.

Benson restricts mixolydian quartal voicings on the V chord to major-resolving contexts only: "on the Vth degree of a minor cadence, we can use all the possibilities we have learned for dominant 7th chords, except with the mixolydian chord voicings, which can only be used when they are leading to major chords." Chapter 7, p. 279.

Benson prohibits using the V degree of a melodic minor scale as a substitute for the dominant when it shares the root of the tonic: "we could not use the C7(9/b13){V degree of F melodic minor} to replace G7, because it has the same root note as the key (Cmaj7), and the cadence would disappear: Dm7, C7(9/b13), Cmaj7." Chapter 2, p. 40.

Benson prescribes using the melodic minor chord family as a resource to substitute for dominant region chords (major or minor subdominant region equivalents): "the chords derived from the melodic minor scale can replace the dominant region chords with the subdominant region chords (major or minor), it means that we can use the melodic minor chord family to replace the dominant region chords." The V degree exception is noted separately. Chapter 2, p. 40.

Benson prescribes replacing a V7 chord with a tonic-root diminished chord in a bass pedal context: the bass stays on the tonic while the chord moves, yielding C° resolving to C6 instead of G7 | C6. "The bass stays the same and the chords move around. Therefore we have: C° resolving to C6." Chapter 2, p. 21.

Benson organizes diminished chords into two functional categories: Fake Diminished (inverted dom7(b9) functioning as a V7 substitute) and Hybrid Diminished (usable as either a connecting chord or a direct V7 substitute in a cadence). Both are dominant-region substitutes. Chapter 2, pp. 19--20.

Benson prescribes exploiting diminished symmetry for substitution: "Diminished Chords have an interesting characteristic, they repeat themselves every minor 3rd. In other words, for every diminished chord, we will always have four options. Example: 'C°' can be replaced by 'Eb°', 'Gb°' or 'A°', because they contain the same notes, therefore are the same chord." Chapter 2, p. 19.

Benson prescribes the Fake Diminished as an inverted dom7(b9) with the root omitted: "This type of diminished chord can be analyzed as an inverted dominant 7th (b9) chord." The root (e.g., A) is removed, leaving the upper structure (b7, b9, 3) which maps to four equivalent diminished voicings, each a usable V7 replacement. Chapter 2, p. 19.

Benson prescribes the Hybrid Diminished chord in two roles: as a connecting chord (passing between chords) or as a substitute for V7 in a cadence. "This type of diminished chord can be analyzed in two different ways: First as a connecting chord, and second as a substitute chord for the V7 degree of a cadence." Chapter 2, p. 20.

Benson includes sus voicings in the dominant tension palette for V7 leading to major: Gsus9, Gsus13, and Gsus(b9) appear alongside standard dom7 tensions. Sus voicings are available dominant-region colour options governed by melody when comping. Chapter 1, p. 2.

Benson prescribes that quartal dom7 voicings for comping should start from the 3rd, 4th, or 5th strings: "we most often use the chords starting from the 3rd, 4th and 5th strings, because the chords rooted from the 6th string might not work. Sometimes, even the chords starting from the 5th string might not work if used in low areas of the instrument." Chapter 6, p. 204.

When dom7 quartal tetrad voicings sound muddy on lower strings, Benson prescribes dropping the lowest note: "some chords on the lower strings might not sound desirable, in these cases we can take out the lower note and play a 3 note quartal voicing." Chapter 7, p. 276. He also notes: "Be careful of the lower notes. They can make the chord sound undesirable." Chapter 7, p. 275.

Benson prescribes memorizing block chord examples rather than constructing them analytically in performance: "they should be memorized and not just analyzed in order to become natural and easy to play." Chord ideas and groove (rhythmic) ideas are treated as independently interchangeable variables. Chapter 7, p. 290.

Benson requires every maj7 voicing concept to be internalized from both the 5th-string root and the 6th-string root: "on the guitar we must learn things considering the 5th string as the root and also the 6th string as the root. Therefore, below we have examples in the keys of 'Cm' (root on the 5th string) and 'Gm' (root on the 6th string)." Chapter 1, p. 11.

As with all chord qualities in this method, Benson prescribes learning minor 7th voicings from both 5th-string and 6th-string root positions, illustrating this with minor key examples in Cm (5th string root) and Gm (6th string root). Chapter 1, p. 11.

Benson prescribes memorizing all dom7 voicing patterns from both 5th-string and 6th-string root positions throughout the chapter exercises. This guitar-specific positional rule is stated as a universal requirement: "on the guitar we must learn things considering the 5th string as the root and also the 6th string as the root." Chapter 1, p. 11.

Benson prescribes that at the I degree (maj7 tonic), only chords from the 1st, 3rd, or 6th columns of the modal interchange table may be substituted: "in every I degree we can use chords belonging from the 1st, 3rd or 6th columns." Chapter 2, p. 29.

At the II degree (IIm7), Benson permits substitutions from the 2nd, 4th, 5th, or 7th columns of the modal interchange table: "in every II degree we can use chords belonging from the 2nd, 4th, 5th or 7th columns." The same columns apply to the IV degree. Chapter 2, p. 29.

At the V degree (dom7), Benson permits substitutions from the 5th, 7th, 2nd, or 4th columns of the modal interchange table: "in every V degree we can use chords belonging from the 5th, 7th, 2nd or 4th columns." Chapter 2, p. 29.

In parallel-mode exercises, Benson requires that the first chord always be drawn from the major key: "the first chord of the sequence will always be from the major key, and all the other chords will be the degrees belonging to the parallel minor key." This rule gives the modal interchange colour its characteristic major-to-minor shift. Chapter 2, p. 33.

When harmonizing a passage over a half-diminished chord using the minor blues scale quartal shape (1, 4, b7), Benson prescribes placing scale notes always in the top voice: "the scale notes will always be on the top voice of each chord. By doing this, we give strength to the chord melody, since they sound like 'power chords' as they contain intervals of a 5th and 4th between each note." Non-scale notes are permitted in inner voices. Chapter 6, p. 244.

Benson prescribes learning all quartal tetrad voicings from every string as a fretboard visualization exercise, not for immediate comping deployment: "Knowing all the possibilities of quartal tetrads starting from each string is part of the fretboard visualization process that we must improve on everyday if we want to improvise and harmonize better." Chapter 6, p. 208.

Benson prescribes modal quartal voicings primarily for static-harmony contexts: "This concept is very useful when we play single chord songs such as 'Impressions', the first part of 'Take Five', 'So What' and 'A Love Supreme'." Over chord progressions, each chord may receive a separate modal quartal treatment, though the major-scale quartal family cannot cover all chord types. Chapter 6, p. 216.

Benson prescribes using bass-note selection to determine modal identity over a fixed quartal chord sequence: "if we play the bass note 'E' continuously over the sequence of chords above, we would have a 'E' Phrygian chord sequence. If we play the bass note 'D' continuously, we would have a 'D' Dorian chord sequence, and so on." Chapter 6, p. 216.

Benson prescribes three practice rules for internalizing quartal triads: (1) never lose the guide chords from view, visualizing each chord by its root note; (2) lower-voiced chords may not work as comping chords; (3) chord symbols for inverted quartal chords use simple letter names. Chapter 6, p. 217.

Benson prescribes the melodic pedal point technique for quartal dom7 voicings: the top voice is held fixed while lower voices shift. "Melodic pedal point is a concept where the lowest voicings of the chords move, but the top voice remains the same." These patterns can be played over any mode from the generating scale. Chapter 6, p. 227.

Benson prescribes memorizing the foundational open-string chord vocabulary before advancing in Chapter 5: "The following chords are considered the most common using open strings. Memorize them and keep following the explanations." Open-string maj7 shapes are among the first-tier vocabulary. Chapter 5, p. 114.

Benson prescribes applying open-string dom7 voicings and pedal-point chords in short harmonic sequences such as I/IVm, I/VI/IIm/V, IV/IVm/I, and I/V: "The best way to use the pedal point chords or any open string chord, is to apply them as much as you can in every situation that is possible. It is advisable to apply them using simple and short sequences." Chapter 5, p. 169.

When an open-string dom7 chord shape is difficult to fret, Benson permits omitting notes to accommodate hand size without destroying harmonic function: "depending on the size of our hand, some chords might be very difficult to play in determined keys. So in order to solve this problem, sometimes we can omit some notes." Chapter 5, p. 112.

When transposing any open-string dom7 shape to other frets, Benson warns that chord quality can shift fundamentally -- a dom7 shape may become another quality entirely: "some chords do not change their characteristics, but others can change completely, going from a major chord to a minor chord at times." The player must verify quality at each fret position. Chapter 5, p. 112.

Benson prescribes that the blues, in its simple form, is harmonically based on dominant 7th chords: "Harmonically, in its simple form, it is based on dominant 7th chords." The blues scale summarizes all the chords in the form. Two forms exist: Major Blues and Minor Blues. Chapter 5, p. 91 (Chapter 4 section).

Benson prescribes a specific method for internalizing blues form dom7 progressions: "Snap your fingers on beats 2 and 4, similar to what the drummer plays on the hi hat, then sing the degrees of each one of the shown blues forms. This is a very important step because we must know these forms inside and out without having to think about them." Chapter 4, p. 91.

Benson prescribes a specific quartal practice protocol for dom7 voicings: study in one key thoroughly before transposing, and memorize only the voicing colours preferred rather than all possibilities: "We strongly recommend to study in one key for sometime, then after visualizing the possibilities in the key you have chosen, go ahead with other keys. Remember that we do not have to memorize all the possibilities presented in this book. Memorize the ones you like." Chapter 6, p. 259.
